note: Surf words glossary. Add new words with an 'added' date; words added in the last 60 days show as New. Words added after 'base' count as new; a word added today becomes the word of the day.

words.d: A peaky wave that breaks both left and right from the same spot, so two surfers can ride it in opposite directions.
The hollow tube a wave makes when its lip throws out over the face. Riding inside it is the most prized thing in surfing.
A wave that breaks over a sand bottom. The peaks move as the sandbars shift.
An unusually big wave in a set, much larger than the rest.
A wave that breaks all at once along its whole length, leaving no open face to ride.
A soft wave where the whitewater spills gently down the face instead of throwing over.
The unbroken front of a wave that surfers ride on.
Smooth, mirror-like water with little or no wind.
Swell made by distant storms. It arrives long-period, powerful and well organised.
Short-period swell made by local wind. It tends to be weaker and choppier than ground swell.
The top edge of a breaking wave that pitches forward.
The area just past the breaking waves where surfers wait for sets.
A wave that breaks to the surfer's left, as seen by a surfer riding toward the beach.
A wave that breaks to the surfer's right, as seen by a surfer riding toward the beach.
Weak, slow waves without much push or shape.
Wind blowing from land out to sea. It holds the wave face up and cleans it, so it is the best wind for surfing.
Wind blowing from the sea onto land. It makes waves messy and crumbly.
The highest point of a wave, where it first starts to break.
A wave that wraps around a headland or point and peels in one direction for a long ride.
A wave that breaks over coral or rock. It is usually consistent and powerful, but shallow.
A group of bigger waves that arrive together, with lulls in between.
The unbroken, gentler part of a wave, out away from the breaking section.
A thick, heavy wave that breaks over a sudden shallow ledge and often sucks below sea level.
Energy travelling across the ocean that becomes waves when it reaches the shore.
The time in seconds between waves in a swell. Longer periods mean more power.
The foamy, broken part of a wave after it has crashed.
Part of a wave that breaks ahead of the surfer. It can be ridden, hit or raced past.
When a wave's lip throws out hard, usually just before it barrels.
A wave that gets steeper and bigger when a reflected wave merges with an incoming one.
Two waves merging into one, making a sudden, heavy, steep wave.
Small, bumpy texture on the water caused by wind.
No surfable waves at all.
When the surf is big, consistent and good.
When the waves are excellent, a step up from pumping.
The area closer to shore than the main line-up, where waves have already broken.
Farther out than the line-up. Surfers shout "outside" to warn that a bigger set is coming.
A strong channel of water flowing back out to sea. Surfers use rips to paddle out, but they are dangerous for swimmers.
A deeper area with no breaking waves, often used for paddling out safely.
The daily rise and fall of the sea. Many breaks work best at a particular tide.
Water rushing back down a steep beach. It can bump into incoming waves.
A move where the surfer launches off the lip, flies above the wave and lands back on it.
An air where the surfer spins around and lands going in the original direction, often riding backwards for a moment first.
A rotating air where the surfer spins toward the back of the wave.
Surfing with your back to the wave face.
Surfing facing the wave.
The first big turn at the bottom of the wave, which sets up every move that follows.
A smooth, powerful turn on the open face that throws spray.
A turn that brings the surfer back toward the breaking part of the wave after they have run out onto the shoulder.
Riding up and across the top of a breaking section, then dropping back down.
Longboard move: standing on the nose with all ten toes over the front edge.
Longboard move: five toes hanging over the nose.
Pulling out of a wave on purpose by turning back over the top.
A turn where the surfer leans far back and drags their body against the wave.
Longboard move: walking to the front of the board and riding from the nose.
Longboard footwork: walking up and down the board by crossing one foot over the other.
Hitting the lip vertically and coming straight back down the face.
A quick, sharp turn off the top that throws spray.
Letting the tail of the board slide out sideways during a turn.
A turn at the top of the wave, after the bottom turn.
Riding inside the barrel of a wave.
Moving up and down on the face to build speed.
Pushing a shortboard under an oncoming wave to get through it while paddling out.
Flipping a longboard upside down and holding on so a wave passes over you.
The fast move from lying on the board to standing.
The steep first descent down a wave face after catching it.
Taking off at the last moment on a steep wave, often while it is already breaking.
A turn that pushes the fins out of the water so the board slides.
An inverted air with an off-axis flip.
A backside air where the surfer grabs the rail and spins around the tail.
Holding the outside edge of the board for control in a barrel or an air.
Backside barrel riding while crouched low and holding the outside rail.
Arching your back with arms loose while riding, purely for style.
Riding with your opposite foot forward.
Swim shorts made for surfing, also called boardies.
The top surface of the board, where you stand.
Small keels under the tail that give grip and control.
A three-fin board setup. It is the most common performance setup.
A four-fin setup that gives speed and drive.
A two-fin setup that is loose and fast, popular in small waves.
One large centre fin. A classic setup on longboards and retro boards.
A short, wide board with a split tail that works well in small, soft waves.
A mid-length board between a shortboard and a longboard. It is easy to paddle.
A long, narrow board built for big waves.
A board about 9 feet or longer, ridden with classic style and noseriding.
A short, light, pointed performance board, usually under about 6 feet 8 inches.
A board around 7 to 8 feet that blends glide and turning.
A soft-top foam board, common for beginners.
A cord that attaches the board to your ankle.
The front tip of the board.
The back end of the board.
The side edge of the board.
The banana-like curve of the board from nose to tail.
A thin strip of wood down the middle of a board that adds strength.
A grippy pad on the tail, also called a tail pad, where your back foot goes.
Sticky wax rubbed on the deck so your feet grip.
A neoprene suit that keeps you warm in cold water.
The craftsperson who designs and shapes surfboards.
A surfer's collection of boards for different conditions.
Damage or a crack in a surfboard.
How much foam a board has, measured in litres. More volume means more float.
A slightly longer board for bigger waves than usual.
Using a jet ski to pull a surfer onto waves too big to paddle into.
A board with a hydrofoil wing underneath that lifts it above the water.
A timed round where 2 to 4 surfers compete against each other.
The right to the next wave in a heat. The surfer with priority wins any wave they choose.
A penalty for blocking or dropping in on a surfer who has the right of way.
A judge-averaged score out of 10 for a single wave.
A surfer's two best wave scores added together, out of 20.
A wave score in the 8 to 10 range.
The highest possible wave score.
When a surfer needs two new scores to take the lead. They are "in a combination situation."
The score a surfer needs on their next wave to take the lead.
A second-chance round where surfers who lost earlier heats can stay in the event.
The knockout round with 16 surfers left, before the quarterfinals.
The round with eight surfers left.
The round with four surfers left, just before the final.
The last heat that decides the event winner.
How surfers are placed into the draw based on ranking.
The window of days an event can run, so organisers can pick the best swell.
A day in the waiting period when the event is paused, often because of poor waves.
The organisers' decision on whether competition runs that day.
The World Surf League's top elite tour, known as the CT.
The World Surf League's qualifying tour for the CT, known as the CS.
The World Surf League's entry-level regional tour, known as the QS.
The ISA's world championship for national teams.
The International Surfing Association, the world governing body for surfing in the Olympics.
ISA points earned by each surfer's finish, added up for their country's team total.
A ranking cut partway through a tour season, after which lower-ranked surfers drop off.
A surfer invited into an event without qualifying through the rankings.
A surfer who takes the spot of an injured surfer.
The combined standings across events or teams.
A clumsy or beginner surfer.
A young surfer, usually a kid.
A clueless surfer, often one who ignores the etiquette.
A surfer who regularly surfs a particular break.
Hostility from locals toward visiting surfers at their break.
Catching a wave that someone else is already riding. It is the biggest etiquette sin.
Paddling around someone to steal their position or wave.
A wave several surfers ride together, on purpose.
Extremely happy and excited, usually after a good surf.
Dangerous, heavy or intense.
A hand sign with thumb and pinky out, meaning hang loose or all good.
Falling off your board, usually hard.
Being held underwater by a wave after a wipeout.
Getting sucked up the face and thrown down with the lip.
When the nose of the board digs underwater and you go flying.
Being stuck in the impact zone while sets break on you.
A surf session.
Surfing at first light, before work or the wind.
So excited to surf that you can barely contain it.
Getting deep inside a barrel.
Another word for getting barreled.
A barrel that blows a burst of spray out of its opening as it closes.
Huge, heavy waves.
Tiny waves.
Excellent conditions or an amazing session.
Relax and take it easy. It is often paired with the shaka.
Really good or impressive.
A surfer who takes on big, dangerous waves without hesitating.
A surfer who travels to follow the best swells.
Where the waves are breaking hardest. It is the worst place to sit.
A tight, quick-dry top that protects against chafing and sun.
A cut from coral or rock. Clean it well, because reef cuts infect easily.
Unwritten rules: the surfer closest to the peak has priority, no dropping in, and don't ditch your board.
Who gets the wave. Usually it is the surfer closest to the peak.
Two surfers racing to paddle into the same wave or position.
A prediction of swell size, period, wind and tide used to plan sessions.
Live swell data from ocean buoys, used to check what is arriving.
A quiet period between sets.
Practice that helps surfers handle long hold-downs in big waves.
A big-wave safety vest that inflates to bring a surfer up after a wipeout.
A spot at the Olympics. Some are won by a surfer by name, others by a country, which then picks who fills it.
An Olympic spot set aside for a surfer from a country with little Olympic history, so the field isn't only the usual surfing nations.
The WSL's regional tour for surfers 20 and under, also called the JQS. The top-ranked juniors in each region earn spots at the World Junior Championships.
Backup days after a contest's planned dates, used if the waves are too poor to finish on time. LA28 Olympic surfing has them.
